title: Joshua 23:1–8
context: Late in life, after the LORD has given Israel rest from its enemies, Joshua gathers the elders, heads, judges, and officers and reminds them that the LORD fought for them and will drive out the nations that remain. He urges them to be very courageous in keeping the book of the law of Moses, to avoid the gods of the remaining nations, and to hold fast to the LORD. Both traditions read this farewell as shared ground: God’s faithfulness grounds the call to wholehearted covenant loyalty.

verses.text: After many days, when the LORD had given rest to Israel from their enemies all around, and Joshua was old and well advanced in years,
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua is old, and the LORD has given Israel rest from its enemies. Arminian readers note that this rest fulfills earlier promises (Josh 21:44; 22:4), yet the chapter will show that it must be guarded by continued faithfulness.

The farewell setting gives Joshua’s words the weight of a leader’s last charge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the rest as God’s gift, won by the LORD rather than by Israel’s strength. Hebrews later says Joshua’s rest was not the final rest God promised (Heb 4:8).

The old leader’s charge points the people beyond himself to the God who gave the rest.

verses.text: Joshua called for all Israel, for their elders and for their heads, and for their judges and for their officers, and said to them, “I am old and well advanced in years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua calls all Israel through its leaders: elders, heads, judges, and officers. Arminian readers note that the whole leadership is made responsible for passing on the charge.

Joshua’s frank “I am old” reminds them that leadership changes, but the covenant remains.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see an ordered covenant community, with leaders accountable for the people’s faithfulness.

Joshua’s awareness of his age turns attention from the human leader to the LORD, who continues when leaders die.

verses.text: You have seen all that the LORD your God has done to all these nations because of you; for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua reminds them that they have seen what the LORD did to the nations, for the LORD fought for them. Arminian readers note that the people’s own experience is the basis of the appeal.

What they have witnessed should shape how they choose to live (cf. Deut 1:30).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the phrase “it is the LORD your God who has fought for you.” Victory was God’s work (cf. Exod 14:14).

Both traditions agree that remembered grace is the ground of the call to obedience.

verses.text: Behold, I have allotted to you these nations that remain, to be an inheritance for your tribes, from the Jordan, with all the nations that I have cut off, even to the great sea toward the going down of the sun.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua has allotted to the tribes both the conquered land and the nations that remain. Arminian readers note that the inheritance is assigned but not yet fully possessed (cf. Josh 13:1–7).

The gift is real, and Israel still has a part to play in taking hold of it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s promise as already settled in the allotment, even where possession is incomplete.

The great sea toward the going down of the sun is the Mediterranean, marking the full extent of the promised inheritance.

verses.text: The LORD your God will thrust them out from before you, and drive them from out of your sight. You shall possess their land, as the LORD your God spoke to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will thrust out the remaining nations, and Israel will possess their land, as he spoke. Arminian readers note that God’s promise and Israel’s possession go together.

The following verses make clear that faithfulness matters for how the promise unfolds.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s word as the guarantee of the future: “as the LORD your God spoke to you.”

The promise rests on God’s faithfulness, which both traditions affirm as the foundation of Israel’s hope.

verses.text: “Therefore be very courageous to keep and to do all that is written in the book of the law of Moses, that you not turn away from it to the right hand or to the left;
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua urges them to be very courageous in keeping all that is written in the book of the law of Moses, turning neither right nor left. Arminian readers hear an echo of the charge given to Joshua himself (Josh 1:7–8).

Courage here is moral: steady obedience against pressure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear Joshua 1:7–8. The written word governs the people’s life.

Not turning to the right or left (cf. Deut 5:32) pictures a straight path set by God’s law rather than by surrounding culture.

verses.text: that you not come among these nations, these that remain among you; neither make mention of the name of their gods, nor cause to swear by them, neither serve them, nor bow down yourselves to them;
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel must not mix with the remaining nations, invoke their gods’ names, swear by them, serve them, or bow to them. Arminian readers note that idolatry often begins with small accommodations (cf. Exod 23:13).

The warning moves step by step from association to worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the first and second commandments applied to life among the nations.

Even speaking the names of other gods in oaths is forbidden, because worship and allegiance are expressed in words as well as acts.

verses.text: but hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day.” Arminian readers note the encouragement: Joshua commends their faithfulness so far and urges them to continue in it.

Perseverance is presented as an ongoing call.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the language of close covenant attachment (cf. Deut 10:20; 13:4).

The call to hold fast is real. Reformed readers also see God’s keeping grace as what enables his people to persevere.
